main.description: A language of the Leksis dictionary, identified by its IETF (BCP 47) tag. Records prove authorship, not ownership: any user may publish a record for any tag, and the AppView treats the latest record for a tag as the current version, archiving previous ones. By convention the record key is the normalized (lowercase) tag.

tag.description: Well-formed IETF BCP 47 language tag, normalized to lowercase (e.g. "br", "br-gw").

translations.description: Names of this language in other languages. Must contain the endonym: an item whose languageID equals this record's tag, giving the language's name in itself.

grammar.description: The grammatical vocabulary this language uses, each atom bound to a label written in this language. Optional: a language with nothing declared stays fully usable, and unbound tags on its entries still render. It must be COHERENT to be indexed: every row above layer 1 may only name atoms, feature names and values this same object binds, no two rows may key the same, a category of two or more atoms must be reachable by removing one inherent feature at a time, a feature is inherent to a category XOR the axis of it, an annotation names a default value iff its category names an axis and no two share one, and a lexicographic label set is used nowhere in the grammatical layers. The retired `axes` and `layout` arrays are refused outright: what they declared now lives on the category and in the eu.leksis.paradigm record. The AppView refuses a version that breaks any of these and keeps the previous one current — not because the vocabulary is wrong (a language may bind anything well-formed, minted or documented) but because the editing interface navigates these relations, so a row hanging off something undeclared can be neither reached nor repaired there. The declared maxLength of every array here is likewise enforced, not advisory.

createdAt.description: Client-declared creation time of this record version.

grammar.description: A language's declared grammatical inventory. Binding is how a language declares what it uses, so these arrays are its vocabulary: what is absent is simply not offered when authoring. Only authored rows are stored — there is no skeleton of unbound atoms, since absence already means unbound. Layer 1 declares the atoms (`pos`, `features`, `values`); layer 2 declares the headword categories they combine into (`inherent`, `categories`), each category naming the feature its forms vary over and the value(s) its own headwords sit at. The shape of the inflection tables is NOT here: it belongs to the eu.leksis.paradigm record, which defines its cells one by one. They share one object because they reference each other: unbinding an atom orphans every higher row that uses it, and one self-contained object means a single write keeps the whole cascade consistent. Two further declarations here are lexicography rather than grammar and take part in no cascade: a feature flagged `lexicographic` (register, domain, editorial usage) and the plain `abbreviations`.

pos.description: Parts of speech this language uses.

features.description: Grammatical feature names this language uses. A feature name must be bound before any of its values can be.

values.description: Feature values this language uses, each stating which feature it is an option of.

inherent.description: Which features are inherent to which category — a property of the word itself, not of one of its forms: aspect is inherent to a Slavic verb, gender to a French noun, while number varies across a noun's forms and is therefore not declared here. This is what a headword can be tagged with, and what the entry editor offers one step at a time.

categories.description: The headword categories this language names: a part of speech plus the inherent feature values that identify a kind of word, each with the abbreviation a reader sees — French "nf." for NOUN + Gender=Fem, where a language that prints "n. f." simply binds the two atoms separately and never adds a row here. A category may also name the feature its forms vary over (its `axis`), and then each abbreviation says which value of that axis the HEADWORD carries: Breton nouns are singular by default, collective-only nouns are collective, and an anv-kadarn stroll is plural with its singulative derived. One category, several headword flavours, one abbreviation each. A category of two or more atoms must be reachable through the `inherent` declarations that build it up.

abbreviations.description: Traditional dictionary abbreviations, standing for no tag at all — "udb." for "un dra bennak". They reference nothing here and nothing references them; they live in this object because a contributor opening "the labels of this language" means one shelf, and splitting a dictionary's front matter across two records would buy nothing.

inherentDeclaration.description: "For this category, this feature is inherent." Both halves are variables and no category is privileged: VERB × Aspect, ADJ × Degree, ADP × Conjugation (Breton conjugates its prepositions) are as ordinary as NOUN × Gender. Since the category is itself a tag, inherence can be declared on a combination — declaring a declension inherent to {NOUN, Gender=Fem} rather than to {NOUN} is what makes the entry editor ask for the gender first. That ordering is a lexicographic judgement, and it is the language's to make.

category.description: The category the feature is inherent to: a single atom this language has bound (a part of speech, or a feature value), or a combination of them.

feature.description: Name of the inherent feature, e.g. "Gender". Must itself be bound in `features`; matched by name, as a value is matched to its feature, so a value minted on a Universal Dependencies feature needs no special case.

categoryDeclaration.description: A headword category this language names, and the abbreviation(s) a reader sees for it. Where a category also names an `axis`, each annotation says which value of that axis its own headwords carry — which is how one category holds several headword flavours, each abbreviated differently: an ordinary Breton noun is cited in the singular, a collective-only noun in the collective, and an anv-kadarn stroll in the plural with its singulative derived by rule. A category never declares the axis's value INVENTORY: that is the layer-1 bound values of the feature, and a paradigm's tables enumerate the cells they print by hand.

category.description: The category being named, e.g. NOUN, or NOUN + Gender=Fem. A single atom is allowed — a part of speech on its own is a headword category like any other — and a combination of two or more must be reachable through the `inherent` declarations that build it up.

axis.description: Name of the feature this category's forms vary over, e.g. "Number". Must itself be bound in `features`, matched by name exactly as an `inherent` declaration matches its own feature, and must NOT be declared inherent to this same category — a paradigm cannot be built from a coordinate that is also a constant. When present, every annotation must name the axis value its headword carries; when absent, none may.

annotations.description: How this language names the category, once per headword flavour. One item and no axis is the ordinary case: a single label for the category. Several items each name a different `default` value of the axis, and each is a labelled tag of its own — the category plus that value — which is what an entry created through it carries.

categoryAnnotation.description: One abbreviation of a category, and the axis value the headwords it names sit at. Same two label halves as `#label`, plus the `default` that makes them distinguishable within one category.

long.description: Full form, written in this language for a reader of it — "anv-kadarn gourel", never "masculine noun".

short.description: Optional abbreviated display form; when present it is shown instead of the full form, which appears on hover.

default.description: The value of this category's `axis` that a headword named by this annotation carries — required when the category names an axis, forbidden when it does not. Must be bound in `values` under that feature; matched by name, so a value minted on a Universal Dependencies feature needs no special case. Several comma-separated values mean a headword spanning them all. Two annotations of one category may not share it: it is what tells them apart.

value.description: Part-of-speech name, e.g. "NOUN". One of Universal Dependencies' 17 tags, or a name this language minted when none of them fits.

scheme.description: Provenance. Absent means the item is documented by Universal Dependencies; otherwise the BCP 47 tag of the language that minted it.

references.description: Where this binding's claim comes from. A UD item's documentation URL is derivable and is not stored; on a minted item the reference is what documents the addition, which is the condition UD's extension licence attaches to it.

feature.description: Feature name, e.g. "Gender" or the layered "Number[psor]". Universal Dependencies requires the form [A-Z][A-Za-z0-9]*(\[[a-z0-9]+\])?.

scheme.description: Provenance. Absent means documented by Universal Dependencies; otherwise the BCP 47 tag of the minting language.

note.description: Free prose about the nature of this item, written in this language for a reader of it — what it covers here, how it differs from a neighbouring one, when a contributor should reach for it. Distinct from the fields beside it: `label` NAMES the item, `references` say where the claim comes from, and this explains the thing itself — what the front matter of a printed dictionary says in a sentence under each heading. Offered here and on a value because those two shapes carry the meaning a label cannot fit, and they are what grammatical features, inflection classes and lexicographic label sets are all made of. Record-only content: the AppView indexes nothing of it, exactly as it indexes nothing of a layout.

lexicographic.description: True when this is a lexicographic label set rather than a grammatical feature: register, domain, editorial usage ("archaic", "neologism", "by extension"). Its values are ordinary tags an entry or a sense may carry, rendering and binding exactly like any other; the flag withholds only participation in the grammatical layers, so such a feature is never inherent to a category, never the axis of one and never part of a category's own bundle — none of those describe it. A record saying otherwise is refused rather than indexed and flagged: the editing interface navigates these relations, so it could not have published one.

feature.description: The feature this value is an option of, e.g. "Gender". Must itself be bound in `features`.

value.description: The value, e.g. "Fem". Universal Dependencies requires the form [A-Z0-9][A-Za-z0-9]*, so a value may begin with a digit; several comma-separated values mean the item spans them all ("Gender=Fem,Masc").

scheme.description: Provenance of the feature/value pair as a whole. Absent means documented by Universal Dependencies; otherwise the BCP 47 tag of the minting language — which is how a value minted on a UD feature is expressed ("Number=Sgv", scheme "br").

note.description: Free prose about the nature of this value, written in this language for a reader of it — what it covers, where its border with a sibling value falls, which words or forms take it. Distinct from `label`, which names it, and from `references`, which say where the claim comes from. Record-only content, indexed nowhere.

abbreviation.description: A traditional dictionary abbreviation: "udb." for "un dra bennak", "s.o." for "someone". A shallow primitive standing for no tag at all — not a feature, not a value, not an option to pick from a list. Its short form is its identity, which is why both halves are required where a label's short form is optional, and why it carries no provenance: the only possible answer would be this language's own lexicographic tradition.

short.description: The abbreviated form — the row's identity, unique within a language.

long.description: What it stands for, written out.

label.description: How this language names the bound item, for a reader of this language — a Breton binding says "anv-kadarn", never "noun".

long.description: Full form — the only required half: a lone form is always the full one.

short.description: Optional abbreviated display form; when present it is shown instead of the full form, which appears on hover.

text.description: The reference's display text (a citation, source name or note).

url.description: Optional URL the reference links to.

languageID.description: BCP 47 tag of the language this name is written in.

translation.description: The language's name written in the language identified by languageID.
